name: Shatt Damam
confidence_why: Boyeldieu 2009, the only first-hand modern description, records two contrastive pitch levels with High occurring at most once per word in a position that shifts with morphology but says it is not yet clear whether the system is tonal or a stress system, and Tucker & Bryan 1966, working from Stevenson's 1950s notes, report three tone levels and an uninvestigated role for stress, so the pitch-based coding is well supported while its exact type is left open by the sources themselves.
catalog_citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2009. The modified form of Shatt Damam nouns and its Daju cognates. Afrika und Übersee 90: 9-84. Author's pre-publication version, HAL halshs-00348145 (submitted 17 Dec 2008; cover: 'À paraître dans Afrika und Übersee'), 51 pp., own pagination; some secondary references (Wikipedia) give 2011, vol. 91; published pagination not verified.
catalog_locator: §2.3 'Prosodic features', preprint p. 3; own name at §1, preprint p. 1. Published Afrika und Übersee pagination not verified.
catalog_quote: Shatt Damam exhibits two constrastive pitch levels, usually transcribed on vowels as follows: Low à vs. High á. However, a contrastive level may also appear on the first component of a strong or geminate nasal (e.g., m̀mágìc (simple form) ‘gum (of trees)’) or on a nasal preceding another consonant (e.g., ŋ̀gánà ‘count! (you pl.)’). High pitch does not normally appear more than once in a single word. Furthermore, its position is not invariant in all morphosyntactic contexts, cf.: gàx (gáxsɨ̀⁺) ‘stick’ gáx àŋ ‘it is a stick’. bà (bánɨ̀⁺) ‘house’ bánɨ̀-mà ‘his house’ ɓùl (ɓúldɨ̀⁺) ‘drum’ ɓùldɨ́-mà ‘his drum’ Rather, it is assigned according to rules which are not fully understood. Finally, it is not yet clear whether this prosodic system should be analyzed as tonal or as a stress system. Although tone/stress is affected in the formation of the modified noun form (e.g., gàx vs. gáxsɨ̀⁺ ‘stick’), it never acts as a conditioning factor in this process.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word carries at most one High pitch (culminative, pitch accent-like) against Low elsewhere; the High is contrastive but its position is not fixed — it moves between morphosyntactic contexts (gàx 'stick' vs gáx àŋ 'it is a stick'; bà 'house' vs bánɨ-mà 'his house') by rules the author could not state, and he explicitly leaves open whether this is a tone system or a stress system. No fixed positional rule can be extracted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the source says High pitch 'does not normally appear more than once in a single word'.
new_statements.exceptions: A contrastive pitch level may also sit on the first part of a geminate nasal or on a preverbal nasal (m̀mágìc 'gum', ŋ̀gánà 'count!'); tone/stress changes accompany the modified (construct) noun form and some plural suffixation (§3); demonstratives trigger a 'regressive tone-raising effect' on the head noun (sìttè 'rope' vs sìtté án 'this rope', p. 26). Data from a single unplanned survey (Khartoum, Jan. 2008); author calls the phonology 'tentative'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (simple vs modified noun forms, citation forms and short phrases); the shifting position of High across contexts (e.g. before -mà 'his', before àŋ copula) suggests a phrase/word-domain interaction the source does not resolve. The community orthography (Alfira et al. 2017) marks neither tone nor stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Boyeldieu's data are from the Shatt Damam dialect (main town Tolle, south of Kadugli); Shatt comprises Shatt Damam, Shatt Tebeldia and Shatt Safia/Safaya dialects (Stevenson 1956-57), none with a separate glottocode — all fall under shat1244. The Alfira et al. Caning materials are for the same language under its own name Caning (Glottolog alternative name).

readall_conflicts: Tucker & Bryan 1966 (from Stevenson's 1950s Shatt material) report three tone levels with no tonal doublets and say stress 'would also seem to have some importance' without investigating it; Boyeldieu 2009 (own fieldwork) finds two contrastive pitch levels (Low vs High), High appearing at most once per word and shifting with morphosyntactic context, and states it is not yet clear whether the system is tonal or a stress system. The two disagree on the number of pitch levels (three vs two) and on whether pitch is contrastive (no doublets found vs contrastive levels), but neither gives a word-stress placement rule and neither classifies the language as a stress language. held by the project: Tucker & Bryan 1966 (Stevenson's data) report three tone levels for Daju (mostly Shatt) with stress 'of some importance' but uninvestigated, while Boyeldieu 2009 sec. 2.3 (the catalog source) describes two contrastive pitch levels with High normally at most once per word and its position morphosyntactically conditioned; the two agree that prosody is pitch-based and neither gives a word-stress placement rule; they differ only in the number of levels (three vs two). The catalog's 'tonal' coding with an empty rule stands.
